query: Prior studies of Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys showed that composition and thermal history can substantially alter constituent phases and transformation behavior, but they did not establish a predictive explanation of phase stability across the relevant thermal regime or adequately connect it to composition-dependent thermodynamic instability. Given the competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors in multicomponent alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state and why? State a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations, boundary conditions, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, the retention of the high‐temperature BCC state versus transformation to secondary phases is controlled by a composition-dependent free energy threshold that, when coupled with slower cooling rates (i.e., sufficient atomic mobility), triggers nucleation and growth of alternate phases.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy homogenized in a high-temperature BCC state
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of the cooling rate from rapid quenching (minimizing atomic diffusion) to slow furnace cooling (allowing diffusion)
generation.conditions: All samples have identical composition and are initially equilibrated at high temperature in the BCC phase; environmental and processing parameters are kept constant except for the cooling rate.
generation.structural_mediator: The onset of atomic-scale diffusion and nucleation events at grain boundaries or within grains that lead to the formation of secondary phases (e.g., FCC or ordered intermetallic phases) once the free energy threshold is met.
generation.mechanism: The alloy’s specific composition sets a free energy difference between the high-temperature BCC phase and lower-energy secondary phases. When the cooling rate is slow, atomic mobility is sufficient to allow overcoming kinetic barriers so that, once the free energy drop exceeds a critical threshold, nucleation and growth of the new phases occur. In contrast, rapid cooling kinetically suppresses diffusion, retaining the BCC structure despite thermodynamic favorability for a transformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples cooled rapidly will largely retain the BCC phase, whereas those cooled slowly will exhibit a significant fraction of secondary phases. An intermediate cooling rate should yield a transitional phase fraction, marking a boundary where the interplay of thermodynamic driving force and kinetic accessibility determines phase stability.
generation.baseline: The intermediate cooling rate sample, which should display a mix of BCC and minor secondary phases, serves as the reference for contrasting the effects of more extreme cooling conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is limited to the high-temperature processing regime where the alloy is in the BCC state; outside this regime the free energy landscape or diffusion mechanisms may differ. In addition, structural heterogeneities or minor compositional fluctuations could shift the effective critical cooling rate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical cooling rate at which the free energy threshold is overcome remains uncertain due to microstructural variability and limitations in free energy predictions. Quantitative phase fractions and exact transformation temperatures may also vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identically composed Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples ensured to be in the high-temperature BCC state. Subject groups of samples to different cooling regimes: rapid quenching, moderate cooling, and slow furnace cooling. Monitor in situ phase evolution using high-temperature synchrotron XRD and post-process the microstructure with SEM/TEM to quantify phase fractions.
measurements: XRD phase identification over time during cooling
Quantitative assessment of the BCC versus secondary phase fraction
Microstructural imaging (SEM/TEM) to assess nucleation sites and phase boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples subjected to rapid cooling exhibit significant secondary phase formation, or if no systematic transition in phase fractions is observed with decreasing cooling rate (i.e., the BCC phase persists even under conditions expected to surpass the free energy threshold), then the hypothesis is invalidated.

However, plenty of nano-particles and platelet-like phases showed up when the sample was cooled in the heat treatment furnace (FC1, Fig. 4(b)). The XRD results, as shown in Fig. 2, indicated that Q1 HEA had mainly FCC phase and minor Laves and R phases while the FC1 HEA was composed of γ′, R, σ, Laves and FCC phases. These results illustrated that a high cooling rate during the solid-state phase transformation can prevent the precipitation of γ′ and σ phases.

decision.trend: Early studies on Al‐containing high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) first used high‐throughput first‐principles calculations coupled with Monte Carlo simulations (as in PMC6207727) to predict multiphase evolution based on composition and temperature. Later, mesoscale modeling (e.g., PMC9498035, where oxidation in an AlCoCrFeNi system was simulated) further demonstrated that complex microstructures and thermal histories affect phase formation. In all cases, the work established that both the thermodynamic driving forces (sensitive to composition) and the kinetic constraints (set by thermal history) are important, yet the precise interplay between these factors in governing phase stability in systems such as Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 remains unquantified.
decision.unsolved: The open gap is that no single, testable mechanistic hypothesis has been established which quantitatively links the composition‐dependent free energy instability with the kinetic limitations imposed by controlled thermal histories (e.g., cooling rates) in defining the phase stability of the high‐temperature BCC state. In other words, it remains unresolved how a threshold in the free energy landscape, when combined with a specific cooling regime, determines whether the alloy retains its BCC state or transforms to secondary phases.
decision.lever: systematic variation of cooling rate (thermal history) on identically composed Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples with in situ high‐temperature synchrotron XRD monitoring
decision.why: Prior simulation and modeling studies indicate that a critical free energy threshold—determined by composition—triggers phase transformation once kinetic diffusion becomes favorable. By varying the cooling rate while keeping composition constant, one can delineate the kinetic domain where the thermodynamic instability is activated. The observation (or lack thereof) of a sharp transition from high-temperature BCC to alternate phases will provide a clear, falsifiable test of the hypothesis that phase stability is governed by the interplay between a composition-dependent thermodynamic threshold and the kinetics of thermal processing.
